So he had experienced it again! When she climbed up to him in the quarry in her yellow dress and blood-red hat, she looked like a wandering butterfly stepping from stone to stone and stopping before him. “I did not wish to disturb you,” she had said, smiling; her smile was red, her whole face lit up, she scattered stars. Fine blue veins had appeared on her neck, and the few freckles under her eyes gave her a warm color. She was in her twentieth year.

A surprise? What was her intention? Did she perhaps mean to show him his books, lay out those two or three volumes, and delight him by saying she had bought them all and cut their pages? “Here you are, a tiny token of attention and kindly consolation! Do not scorn my humble contribution!”

He rose abruptly and stood still. Victoria returned; her basket was empty.

“You found no flowers?” he asked absently.

“No, I gave it up. Nor did I look; I merely sat there.”

He said:

“While I remember: you must not go on thinking you have done me some wrong. You have nothing to make amends for with any sort of kindly consolation.”

“No?” she answered, taken aback. She thought further, looked at him, and pondered. “No. I thought that, that time ... [the source OCR reads ‘+++’] I did not want you always to go on bearing a grudge against me for what happened.”

“No, I bear you no grudge.”

She thinks for another moment. Suddenly she draws herself up.

“Then that is well,” she says. “No, I ought to have known. It did not leave so great an impression. Well, then, we shall say no more about it.”

“No, let us not. My impressions mean as little to you now as before.”

“Goodbye,” she said. “Goodbye for now.”

“Goodbye,” he answered. [The source OCR contains a vertical stroke.]

They went their separate ways. He stopped and turned. There she went now. He stretched out his hands and whispered, saying tender words to himself: “I bear you no grudge; no, no, I do not; I still love you, love you ...”

“Victoria!” he called.

She heard it, started, and turned, but continued walking.

Several days passed. Johannes went about in the greatest agitation and neither worked nor slept; he spent nearly the whole day in the forest. He climbed the great pine-covered mound where the Castle’s flagpole stood; a flag was flying. A flag had also been raised on the Castle’s round tower.

A strange tension seized him. Guests were coming to the Castle; there was to be a celebration.

The afternoon was still and warm; the river ran like a pulse through the hot landscape. A steamer glided toward the shore and left a fan of white lines across the bay. Now four carriages drove from the Castle courtyard and took the road down to the landing.

The ship docked; ladies and gentlemen came ashore and took their places in the carriages. Then a volley of shots began to crack from the Castle. Two men stood in the round tower, loading and firing hunting guns, loading and firing. When they had discharged twenty-one shots, the carriages rolled through the castle gate and the firing ceased.

Yes, there was to be a celebration at the Castle; the guests were received with flags and a salute. Some soldiers sat in the carriages; perhaps Otto, the lieutenant, was among them.

Johannes descended from the mound and set off homeward. A man from the Castle caught up with him and stopped him. The man carried a letter in his cap; Miss Victoria had sent him and required an answer.

Johannes read the letter with a pounding heart. Victoria was inviting him after all, writing warm words and asking him to come. This time she wished to invite him herself. An answer was to be sent with the messenger.
